Team validated that prefix caching yielded the largest immediate cost reduction for their conversational prompt-patterns (~40% effective token savings on repeats), batching gave 2.1x throughput but increased p99 latency beyond their 300ms SLO in the large-response path, and 8-bit quantization improved tokens/sec by ~1.8x with small quality regression. transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-12
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Rivermark Head of ML), Elena Gomez (Rivermark Platform Eng), Matt O'Leary (Rivermark CTO)

Summary (auto): Weekly POC check-in: pilot economics and perf tuning. Discussed token/sec per dollar, caching savings, batching vs latency, quantization tradeoffs. Action items captured.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep this tight — agenda is tokens per dollar, caching numbers, batching tradeoffs, and next steps. Priya and I ran the extra bench last night.
[00:18] Samir: Cool, thanks. We have a couple of US/UK engineers on calls but they'll jump in if needed. Main focus: lower our inference cost without sacrificing the user experience.
[00:30] Priya: Quick note — I uploaded the run results into the shared folder, file name rivermark_bench_20261011.csv, there's a short readme. The important bits: base hosted config baseline is about 9.6k tokens/dollar on single-stream low-latency mode. With batching at batch size 32 we saw throughput jump, tokens/sec/$ increased to about 19k tokens/dollar, so roughly 2x, but p99 latency went from ~220ms to ~410ms on long responses.
[01:02] Elena: That p99 is worrying for our chat product, we target 300ms interactive. How much of the workload is long responses vs short?
[01:10] Samir: Roughly 30% are >150 tokens, those bump p99. Most are short 20–40 token responses.
[01:18] Priya: Good point. We tried adaptive batching - separate queues for short vs long. For short-only traffic batching gives near 2.4x tokens/dollar and p99 stays under 250ms. For mixed traffic you need smart routing. Redwood's runtime supports request routing by policy so you can keep short flows on low-latency pool and batch long flows.
[01:40] Matt: Can you remind me of the cost delta between hosted and dedicated for that config? If we move to dedicated pools with 2 reserved instances what's the unit economics?
[01:48] Jordan: On the sheet I sent, dedicated reserved for this workload looks like 30–40% cheaper per token assuming you commit to 3 months and use burst scaling. I'll re-send the calc after adjusting for your expected QPS. That's one of the next steps.
[02:03] Priya: On caching: the prefix caching we set up for repeated system prompts saved about 42% of passed tokens in the sample repeat-pattern set Samir shared — that's big. KV cache (per-session KV) saved about 28% in reranking flows. Both help but they apply to different access patterns.
[02:24] Samir: 42% is huge. Is that stable? I mean, what's the hit rate variance?
[02:30] Priya: Hit rate depends on repeat frequency. In our sample set hit-rate was ~65% for prefix caching because many messages start with identical system prompts and templates. For KV, hit-rate was lower but still meaningful for multi-turn summaries. We can run a larger 48h trace to get confidence.
[02:46] Elena: Any quality impact from caching or quant? We can't afford hallucination uptick.
[02:52] Priya: Prefix caching doesn't change model outputs when the cached portion is identical; it's strictly a token-saving optimization. Quantization is where you might see quality shifts. We tried 8-bit dynamic quant — tokens/sec went up ~1.8x, CPU/GPU utilization was better, but spot checks on 200 prompts showed a small increase in n-gram differences, negligible for most flows but risky for some high-precision outputs.
[03:20] Samir: For our compliance docs summary flow we need high fidelity — maybe avoid quant on that route. Can we route that to a higher-quality unquantized endpoint?
[03:28] Jordan: Absolutely — Redwood supports model variants and routing policies. You can pin that route to the FP16 variant and less aggressive batching.
[03:35] Matt: About batching — is it continuous batching? I want to know jitter implications.
[03:40] Priya: Redwood uses continuous batching with adaptive timers. For bursty traffic there can be a small micro-jitter; p50 unaffected, p99 can slip if you push long tails into a batch. That's why we recommend two-tier routing or dynamic batch windows.
[03:55] Samir: Any numbers on tokens/sec/$ when combining prefix caching and batching? Is the effect additive?
[04:00] Priya: In our tests, prefix caching reduced billed tokens by ~42%. If you then batch the remaining live tokens you get the batch multiplier on that reduced base. Practically we saw an effective tokens/dollar of about 31k in short-only heavy-repeat runs (prefix cache + batch size 32, quant off).
[04:20] Elena: So 31k vs baseline 9.6k is big. But that's a best-case with high repeat. Our real-world will be lower.
[04:27] Priya: Correct — it's workload dependent. That's why we want the 48h production-like run to estimate expected hit-rate and stability.
[04:36] Jordan: Also flagged — tokenization differences matter. If you shift prompt templates small changes change token counts; Samir's engineering team should standardize templates to maximize cache hits.
[04:46] Samir: We'll put that into the prompt hygiene task.
[04:49] Matt: On security — Elena had raised KMS and audit logs. Are those ready for Private or Dedicated?
[04:56] Jordan: Private supports customer-managed KMS and full audit logs; Dedicated has options for KMS integration and audit export. We'll surface SOC2 docs and KMS integration guide. Elena, you'll open the ticket?
[05:07] Elena: Yep, I will. Also want to confirm egress and VPC peering details for our on-prem edge.
[05:13] Priya: We documented the VPC peering steps in the README. There was a note about keeping health-check ports open. I'll paste the snippet into the ticket.
[05:22] Samir: Anything on fallbacks? Want to avoid a total outage.
[05:25] Jordan: Redwood supports automated fallback to a cheaper model variant or a different region. We recommend canary routing: 1% of traffic to the new config, monitor latency and quality, then ramp. We can help set up the canary script and alert thresholds.
[05:40] Priya: For the canary, we'll instrument both tokens/sec/$ and a small eval set to monitor quality regression. Suggest rolling canary for the quantized path first with traffic steering.
[05:50] Elena: What about observability? Do we get token-level cost breakdown per route?
[05:54] Jordan: Yes — Redwood Console has per-route token/cost, p50/p95/p99 latency, and trace links. We'll give you a short demo if you want.
[06:03] Samir: Okay, let's come back to concrete numbers — anything surprising in the last run?
[06:07] Priya: One oddity: a small subset of prompts with lots of embedded code caused tokenization to blow up (3x expected tokens) — that skewed cost for that user segment. We recommend pre-tokenization checks in your input pipeline to cap accidental long tokens.
[06:23] Matt: Good call. We'll add a sanitize step.
[06:26] Priya: Also observed that reranker flows benefited more from KV caching than prefix caching; reranker had high repeated context across short sessions.
[06:34] Samir: Any action needed on our infra side to support KV cache?
[06:38] Priya: No infra changes required for hosted; for Dedicated there is a config toggle and a small mem allocation per worker. Priya: (laugh) sorry, that was me repeating.
[06:47] Jordan: (laughs) 
[06:48] Samir: Are there recommended defaults for memory allocations?
[06:51] Priya: For your expected session count we recommend 6GB per worker for KV in ded-2x config; I'll include the calc in the ticket.
[06:59] Elena: Timeline question: if we decide to go Dedicated, how long to provision?
[07:02] Jordan: Typical lead time is 2–3 weeks for reserved pools with networking and IAM wrapped. Private deployment can be longer (4–6 weeks). For a fast start we can do hosted + reserved capacity to emulate Dedicated economics sooner.
[07:16] Samir: OK. Let's sync on the canary and the 48h run. Also want an ROI estimate if we commit to 6 months dedicated.
[07:24] Jordan: I'll run the numbers and share two scenarios: 3-month and 6-month commit with and without prefix caching hit-rate assumptions.
[07:31] Priya: I'll kick off the 48h run later today. Samir, please upload the full trace when available.
[07:36] Samir: Will do.
[07:38] Elena: Quick question — any competitor lock-in risks? We mentioned GoliathAI internally. How portable are these optimizations?
[07:45] Jordan: Prefix and KV caching concepts are portable; the exact APIs are Redwood-specific but we provide migration notes. Quantization formats could differ between runtimes. We'll include a migration doc.
[07:57] Matt: Great. If there's nothing else, let's capture the follow-ups.
[08:00] Jordan: Recap: Priya runs 48h test and uploads logs; Jordan sends pricing and commit scenarios; Samir provides prompts and trace; Elena opens SOC2/KMS ticket. We'll reconvene after results, target 2026-10-19 for a short follow-up.
[08:18] Samir: Thanks everyone.
[08:20] Jordan: Thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.
